state.case_summary:
A 56-year-old man was referred for evaluation of a recurrent skin lesion on the dorsum of his right thumb. He reported a four-year history of a lesion at that site, for which a partial amputation of the thumb was performed in December 2016. In August 2017, the lesion reappeared at the distal aspect of the thumb stump. He had no significant medical history and took no medications. On examination, there was a 1.8 × 1.3 cm well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender, indurated lesion over the dorsum of the right thumb stump that was mobile over the deep structures. No palpable lymphadenopathy was noted. A metastatic workup—including CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and a bone scan—revealed an enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node presumed to represent metastatic disease. The patient was scheduled for a wide local excision with amputation at the level of the distal interphalangeal joint and fine-needle aspiration of the axillary node.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. EccrinePorocarcinoma
B. Basal cell carcinoma was considered because the lesion can mimic its nodular appearance
C. Squamous cell carcinoma was considered due to similar ulcerative, nodular skin lesions
D. Seborrheic keratosis was considered because of its potential for a verrucous plaque
E. Superficial spreading melanoma was considered as part of the spectrum of pigmented malignant lesions
F. Fibroma was considered given the possibility of a benign fibrous mass on the hand
G. Intraepidermal poroma was considered as a benign sweat gland neoplasm
H. Pyogenic granuloma was considered because of its vascular, rapidly growing nature
